about.title: About Me
about.content: Most of what I've shipped, people never see. The data grid that got virtualized because the old one folded at a few thousand rows, the billing flow that refuses to send half a batch of invoices, the monorepo test command that had been silently skipping 13 packages. I work mostly on the frontend, but I write the migration and the API contract too, because that is usually where the bug turns out to be. Seven years of this, from Ribeirão Preto, currently building healthcare software with a team in the United States.

personal.title: Personal
personal.content: I read constantly, mostly other people's postmortems and architecture writeups. The gym happens on a schedule I actually keep. Side projects are how I learn: Fortuna and Mindforge both started as something I wanted and could not find.

technical.title: Technical
technical.content: React, TypeScript and Node across the stack, plus Lit and Web Components where a design system has to outlive the framework that created it. Most of my time goes to the things that are expensive to retrofit: accessibility and render performance, and getting the API contract right the first time.

languages.title: Languages
languages.content: Portuguese is native. English is the language I work in: standups, code review and design discussion, every day since the start of 2025, with a team split between Brazil and Arizona.

tas.title: Software Engineer
responsibilities: Own features end to end on a U.S. healthcare SaaS platform, including inventory-logistics flows and a full billing suite, writing the Postgres migrations, core-api services, domain events, and API contracts, then carrying each through to accessible production UI.

Built foundational pieces of the design system the entire platform ships on: the data grid, select, dialogs, and the virtualized select and grid that fixed a platform-wide performance ceiling. Maintain it with accessibility and performance as hard requirements for every component, and I'm currently fitting the platform to a phone.

Fix reliability holes that only surface under partial failure, including a bug where notification failures could roll back the business writes that triggered them, and an atomicity gap that left orphaned records when PDF generation failed. Made multi-invoice sending all-or-nothing, so a rejected batch changes nothing and names every offender, and tested it by inducing real S3 outages.

Own testing across the stack: Playwright integration, page, API, and visual-regression suites. Fix the test infrastructure itself, including a monorepo test command that was silently skipping 13 packages.

Publish the shared npm packages that keep UI consistent across product teams, and review frontend PRs for architecture and fidelity to Figma designs. Improve the team's AI-assisted workflows with automated code review on every PR and a hierarchical knowledge base that keeps coding agents productive, and cut CI time with parallelized monorepo builds.

freelance.title: Frontend Software Engineer
responsibilities: Built the landing pages and application UI for an ed-tech platform with 1,000+ students, and those pages drove thousands of conversions.
Streamlined student and admin workflows, removing manual steps from day-to-day operations.
Established the frontend architecture around React, React Query, and React Hook Form so the codebase stays maintainable as the product grows.
Worked directly with product stakeholders to turn business requirements into features we could actually ship.

bymycell.title: Software Engineer
responsibilities: Built the React dashboards and reports that turn raw genomics lab results into something researchers can actually read.
Connected frontend and backend systems to make lab workflows traceable end to end, with fewer manual handoffs and errors.
Refactored 6+ legacy backend modules into a DDD architecture while keeping the old system running, without interrupting lab operations.
Added the unit and integration test suites the codebase was missing.

take.title: Frontend Software Engineer
responsibilities: Built and owned the backoffice that runs a network of 1,000+ smart retail coolers: order management, inventory control, promotions, fiscal reporting, and live operational dashboards used daily by internal teams and licensed operators.

Shipped the planogram builder behind a greenfield connected-cooler platform: drag-and-drop shelf composition, stackable product modeling, live door preview, and fleet-wide rollout scored against a computer-vision compliance model.
Ran releases for both products, reviewing and merging 274 pull requests to trunk, 75% of all merges on the newer platform, and owning the production hotfix path.
Wrote the frontend architecture standard the team built against: clean architecture with ports and adapters, the engineering conventions, and the definition of done.
Largest contributor to the shared design system, roughly 70 React and TypeScript components documented in Storybook and reused across teams.
Introduced end-to-end testing with Cypress, so bugs showed up before a deploy instead of after one, then extended CI to run the suite in parallel through Docker builds to AWS ECR.
Created accessible, interactive data visualizations for day-to-day operational decisions, covering sales, execution, demographics, and energy consumption.

suave.title: Full-stack Developer
responsibilities: Shipped 10+ client websites and Next.js landing pages where load speed and conversion were the whole brief.
Designed and built a multi-tenant link-aggregator platform (React + Express) serving multiple client brands from a single codebase.
Developed custom site features that turned client websites into lead-generation channels.
Ran SEO and performance work that lifted clients' organic visibility.

projects.title: Projects & Contributions
projects.subtitle: Products and open-source work I've built and contributed to

fortuna.title: Fortuna
fortuna.description: A personal finance app that keeps spending, cards, parcelas, investments and goals in one place, with an AI co-pilot that reads your bank statements, flags surprises, and answers in plain language. Built for Brazil (BRL, CDI, parcelas) and fully bilingual.

mindforge.title: Mindforge
mindforge.description: A learning tool that turns a topic into a fundamentals-first curriculum, then has an agent write each lesson on demand as you work through it. Three trackers report how far, how much, and how often you have studied, without streaks or invented percentages to inflate the numbers. Built as a TypeScript monorepo with a React front end, a NestJS API, and a Supabase backend.

modularGameStore.title: Modular Game Store
modularGameStore.description: A micro-frontend e-commerce platform built with Rspack and Module Federation, as a working example of frontend architecture that scales across large distributed teams.

marketPulse.title: Market Pulse
marketPulse.description: A real-time financial market monitoring platform using Lit, Lit Signals, Rspack, and Module Federation, written to see how reactive UIs hold up under streaming data loads.

animavita.title: Animavita
animavita.description: Trigger life-saving alerts, register animals for adoption and find the nearest pet looking for a home. An open-source project with 739+ stars and 318+ forks on GitHub.

interests.title: Positions
interests.subtitle: What I currently believe about building software.

positions.accessibility: A component that is not keyboard operable is not done. It is a bug with a nice hover state.
positions.designSystems: A design system does not pay for itself until a second product uses it; before that it is a component folder with extra meetings.
positions.seams: The interesting bugs live at the seams: between the migration, the domain event and the render. That is why I refuse to own only one side of the stack.
positions.tests: The only test I fully trust is one I watched fail before I fixed the bug. I have induced real S3 outages to get that signal.
positions.agents: Coding agents are limited by the context you hand them, which is why I read most complaints about what the AI cannot do as complaints about how hard the repo is to read.
positions.performance: Nobody opens a ticket because a page is merely slow, so performance work only happens when someone decides to care about it without being asked.

changedMyMind.consistency: I used to think a design system's job was visual consistency. Now I think its job is to make the accessible, fast choice the easiest one to reach for.
changedMyMind.coverage: End-to-end tests used to be about coverage for me. Now I keep the handful that cover flows which cost real money when they break, and delete the rest.
